items.t: Банки прогнозируют сильный рост китайских акций к 2027 году
sum: PrimaMedia, 27 ноября. Leading financial experts predict significant upside for Chinese equities in 2027. Despite short-term market volatility, resilient corporate earnings and attractive valuations make these stocks highly appealing for medium— and long-term investors.

Analysts from a major Swiss financial institution expect the MSCI China Index to reach 76 by the end of 2027, implying a 13 percent upside. They note that recent corrections have made technology stocks attractive again, as their prices had significantly deviated from fundamentals. The adjustment in artificial intelligence-oriented tech stocks exceeded the slowdown in corporate earnings expectations. Earnings per share for the MSCI China Index are projected to rise 10 percent next year.

The growth-oriented ChiNext Index recently traded at 24.72 times earnings. According to a prominent market tracker, it has been cheaper on less than 1 percent of trading days since its launch in 2010. Another major global bank forecasts a 23 percent rise for the MSCI China Index and a 10 percent gain for the CSI 300 Index of mainland A shares in 2027. Experts see strong opportunities in companies serving the domestic AI market, as well as in banks and firms raising dividends or buying back shares. Hong Kong-listed shares are currently favored over A shares due to stronger earnings prospects and more attractive valuations.

On Thursday, the mainland benchmark Shanghai Composite Index edged up 0.01 percent to close at 3,476.88 points. The ChiNext Index rose 0.29 percent and the Hang Seng Index gained 1.19 percent. Meanwhile, regulators are stepping up support for equities. The minimum margin requirement for margin trading will be cut on Monday, potentially bringing about 400 billion yuan into the A-share market.

Macroeconomic measures are also underway. The national central bank injected a net 401 billion yuan through open market operations on Wednesday to ease funding pressures. Interest rates remain low and have become less volatile around month— and quarter-end periods. Furthermore, experts remain bullish on the artificial intelligence sector, citing its transformative potential and the early stage of its diffusion across enterprises and households.

sum: Asian equity markets recovered Thursday, November 26, 2026, as technology shares rallied across South Korea, Japan and other regional exchanges following Wall Street's partial recovery. Investors also assessed fresh US trade tariffs and persistent inflation concerns, while uncertainty surrounding artificial intelligence spending continued to influence market sentiment.

South Korea's Kospi climbed 1.73%, while the small-cap Kosdaq gained 2.32%. Japan's Nikkei 225 advanced 1.21%, and the Topix rose 0.71%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng added 1.46%, mainland China's CSI 300 increased 0.12%, and Australia's S&P/ASX 200 gained 0.15%, according to market data reported by CNBC.

Technology companies led the recovery after experiencing substantial selling pressure during the previous session. Japanese investment group SoftBank surged more than 11%, while chip-testing equipment manufacturer Advantest advanced 7.3%. Lasertec and Disco each gained more than 6%, and Tokyo Electron rose 4.6%.

South Korean semiconductor manufacturers also posted strong gains. SK Hynix shares advanced more than 4%, while Samsung Electronics climbed 2.1%. Japanese chipmaker Kioxia also recorded a double-digit increase, according to market coverage published by Yahoo Finance.

The recovery followed several volatile trading sessions driven by concerns about the scale of artificial intelligence investment and uncertainty over when substantial spending would generate returns. Market participants also considered rising interest rate expectations and potential tighter regulation of artificial intelligence under a new Democrat-led Congress.

South Korea's central bank raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 3.25%, its highest level in two years. The Bank of Korea made the adjustment during its final policy meeting of the year as inflation remained above its target and economic growth provided room for tighter monetary policy, CNBC reported.

Cryptocurrency prices also moved higher. Bitcoin gained 1.58% to $60,944.60, while ether increased 1.15% to $1,702.96. However, concerns about the digital asset market persisted after BitMEX co-founder Arthur Hayes told CNBC that bitcoin could test $50,000 if the Nasdaq continued declining.

sum: On November 25, losses in China's A-share market widened significantly in the afternoon session, with all three major indices closing lower and the Shanghai Composite falling below the 3,500-point threshold. At the close, the Shanghai Composite Index stood at 3,476.47, down 2.03%; the Shenzhen Component fell 3.24%; the ChiNext Index dropped 4.19%; and the STAR 50 Index declined more than 5%.

Combined turnover across the two exchanges for the full day reached 1.38 trillion yuan (approximately $207 billion), a shrinkage of 272 billion yuan (approximately $40.8 billion) from the previous trading day. At the individual stock level, declines were broad-based, with 4,926 stocks across the market closing lower and only 586 gaining, of which 57 hit the daily limit up and 44 hit the limit down. Compared with the midday picture, when more than 2,800 stocks were in positive territory, the afternoon correction widened markedly, leaving fewer than 600 stocks in the green at the close.

Sector performance diverged sharply. The chip supply chain fell across the board, with Hua Hong Semiconductor (688347.SS) and Metax (688802.SS) dropping more than 10%, while NAURA Technology (002371.SZ) and Fortune Precision (688409.SS) followed lower. The battery supply chain weakened in tandem, with Shangtai Technology (001301.SZ) hitting the limit down and CATL (300750.SZ) and Shangshui Intelligent declining. Robotics concept stocks also came under pressure, with Beiwei Technology hitting the limit down and SWANCOR Advanced Materials falling more than 10%.

Pharmaceuticals and retail emerged as the few bright spots on the board. The anti-flu segment led the gains, with Kangzhi Pharmaceutical (300086.SZ), Tuoxin Pharmaceutical (301089.SZ), Hubei Hengdi Pharmaceutical (301211.SZ), Shuanglu Pharmaceutical (002038.SZ) and Teyi Pharmaceutical (002728.SZ) among multiple stocks hitting the limit up. In the retail sector, Hangzhou Jiebai (600814.SS) notched a third consecutive limit-up session, while Nanjing Central Emporium (600280.SS), Guofang Group (601086.SS) and Jiajiayue (603708.SS) hit the limit up. Tax-refund store concept stocks were active, with Wanshili recording a 20% limit-up gain.

items.t: NQ: Фьючерсы на Nasdaq приостановились после роста на 6,5%, возвращение Nvidia спровоцировало глобальное ралли
sum: Asian chip stocks soar after Jensen Huang’s return, while a firm dollar and renewed Fed tightening bets complicate the recovery ahead of US inflation data.

- Nasdaq-100 futures NQ slipped 0.3% Tuesday, while S&P 500 futures were broadly flat. The pause follows Monday’s dramatic recovery, when the Nasdaq Composite jumped 6.51% to 24,089.56, the S&P gained 4.73% and the Dow rose 3.01%, for the best day since April 2025.

- Nvidia drove the turnaround after reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO following Trump’s intervention. Shares surged 31.5%, their biggest daily percentage gain since 2003. The move added nearly $1 trillion to the company’s market cap.

- Buying spread across the technology complex. The semiconductor index gained 14%, while Meta climbed 6.6%, Alphabet rose 6.3% and Amazon added 3.5%. That breadth strengthened Monday’s recovery, but sustaining those gains will require investors to look beyond the initial response to Huang’s return.
- Taiwan’s benchmark jumped nearly 10%, with TSMC and Foxconn approaching their daily upward limits. Japan’s Nikkei gained as much as 5%, while South Korea’s Kospi advanced around 6.5%.

- China participated less enthusiastically. The CSI 300 edged higher, while Hong Kong shares slipped 0.4%, reflecting concerns about tighter US chip-export restrictions. European futures were also subdued.

- The recovery revived expectations of Fed tightening. The US two-year Treasury yield stood near 4.67%, with the 10-year around 4.92%. A stronger equity market eases financial conditions, potentially giving policymakers more room to raise rates while inflation remains above target.

items.t: Ралли Nvidia поднимает акции азиатских производителей микросхем и акции Micron
sum: A powerful rebound in artificial intelligence stocks lifted global equity markets on Monday, November 23, 2026, after Nvidia shares surged 31% following Jensen Huang's return as CEO. The rally extended into Asian trading on Tuesday, boosting semiconductor manufacturers and strengthening expectations for continued demand for advanced computing hardware.

According to CNBC, US stock futures continued climbing on Tuesday morning. Nasdaq-100 futures gained 0.19%, S&P 500 futures advanced 0.26%, and Dow Jones Industrial Average futures rose 65 points, or 0.13%.

The previous session delivered substantial gains across Wall Street. The Nasdaq Composite jumped 6.5%, the S&P 500 advanced 4.7%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 3%. These represented the strongest single-session performances for the Nasdaq and S&P 500 since April 9, 2025.

Technology stocks led the recovery, with the S&P 500 technology sector climbing 9%. Micron Technology gained 19%, Advanced Micro Devices added nearly 7%, and artificial intelligence infrastructure company CoreWeave surged 22%.

The rebound also restored confidence among major semiconductor manufacturers across Asia. Taiwan's TSMC and Hon Hai Precision Industry each approached their 10% daily price limits, while MediaTek gained approximately 10%. South Korea's Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix advanced around 8% and 10%, respectively.

South Korea's Kospi climbed more than 7% during Tuesday trading, while Japan's Nikkei 225 advanced 4.05%. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 gained 1.62%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index slipped 0.39%, while mainland China's CSI 300 rose 0.57%.
Glen Smith, chief investment officer at GDS Wealth Management, attributed the recovery partly to reduced uncertainty surrounding Nvidia's leadership and the broader artificial intelligence sector.

items.t: Азия активизирует усилия по спасению запасов, поскольку Китай смягчает правила заимствования
sum: China will lower the minimum margin requirement for securities purchases to 80% from 100% on November 30. South Korea and Taiwan have also announced measures to support markets after a plunge in US equities and steep losses across the region.

China will lower its minimum margin requirement for securities purchases to 80% from 100% on November 30, as Asia’s stock rescue efforts gather pace. South Korea and Taiwan have also announced measures following a plunge in US equities.

The Chinese change lets investors buy securities with less money of their own when borrowing from a brokerage. South Korea plans a stock stabilization fund, while Taiwan has tightened restrictions on short sales and bought shares.

The Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing stock exchanges announced the margin change with approval from the China Securities Regulatory Commission. The exchanges had raised the requirement to 100% from 80% in January to curb borrowing risks.

Regulators said margin-financing activity had fallen markedly and overall borrowing levels were relatively low. The securities watchdog said this month that those conditions created room to adjust risk controls.

Brokerages can apply the revised rules to existing financing contracts when calculating available margin balances. Investors involved in abnormal trading may face stricter requirements and other risk controls.
China’s benchmark CSI 300 Index fell more than 8% in October, its worst monthly performance in more than a decade. Economic weakness and a sharp reversal in technology shares weighed on sentiment.

items.t: Усилия по спасению акций в Азии набирают обороты после обвала Уолл-стрит
sum: Asian authorities are stepping up efforts to stem a deepening stock-market rout, with China easing margin requirements, and Taiwan and South Korea rolling out intervention measures following Friday’s plunge in US equities.

In China, the minimum margin requirement for investors buying securities with borrowed funds will fall to 80% from 100% on Nov. 30, according to notices issued on Sunday by the Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing stock exchanges with approval from the China Securities Regulatory Commission. The exchanges had raised the ratio to 100% from 80% in January to curb leverage risks.

Regulators said the latest adjustment is related to a marked decline in margin-financing activity and relatively low overall leverage. Brokerages can apply the revised rules to outstanding financing contracts when calculating available margin balances, while investors engaged in abnormal trading may face stricter requirements and other risk controls.
The change could unleash nearly 400 billion yuan in additional funds, the Xinhua News Agency reported Sunday, citing the regulator.

The moves add to a series of efforts by Beijing to restore confidence after a months-long rout pushed the benchmark CSI 300 Index into a bear market. The gauge tumbled over 8% in October, its worst monthly performance in more than a decade, as weakness in the economy and a sharp reversal in tech shares weighed on sentiment.

Also on Sunday, South Korea announced phased measures to calm markets amid rising volatility. The moves include ensuring a stock stabilization fund is in place to respond when needed, top financial officials said after an emergency meeting.

Earlier, Taiwan widened curbs on short sales of local stocks and said it has been buying shares, stepping up efforts to revive confidence after the island’s benchmark index had its worst weekly fall in 35 years.

sum: Global stock markets recorded sharp declines during the week, with major US stock indices losing nearly 8–12% of their value, while selling pressure also intensified in European and Asia-Pacific markets, APA-Economics reports.
During the trading week ending November 20, the US Dow Jones index fell by 8.03%, the S&P 500 declined by 8.61%, and the Nasdaq Composite dropped by 11.89%.

On November 20 alone, the Dow Jones index fell by 949.73 points, or 1.93%, to 48,147.33 points. The S&P 500 declined by 265.44 points, or 3.70%, to 6,910.39 points, while the Nasdaq Composite dropped by 1,261.47 points, or 5.28%, to 22,617.73 points.
The NYSE Composite index fell by 2.08% to 22,657.82 points, while Canada's S&P/TSX Composite index declined by 2.47% to 33,189.85 points.
All major European stock indices also recorded declines. The Euro Stoxx 50 index fell by 2.81% to 5,941.95 points, while the UK's FTSE 100 declined by 1.02% to 10,346.34 points.
Germany's DAX index dropped by 2.60% to 24,802.78 points, France's CAC 40 fell by 1.89% to 7,927.75 points, and Spain's IBEX 35 declined by 1.63% to 18,873.10 points.
All major indices in the Asia-Pacific region also declined. Japan's Nikkei 225 index fell by 3,007.56 points, or 5.06%, to 56,436.65 points, while the TOPIX index dropped by 3.88% to 3,674.22 points.

sum: Growing concerns about the profitability of artificial intelligence investments triggered another wave of selling across global markets on Friday, November 20, 2026, as Asian equities headed toward their steepest weekly decline since 2020. Anthropic's highly anticipated Nasdaq debut failed to restore investor confidence, while major chipmakers and technology stocks recorded further losses.
According to CNBC, Anthropic shares fell 5.6% in premarket trading at 4:23 a.m. ET on Friday. Nvidia declined 1.66%, while Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) dropped 4.12% during the same session.

The retreat followed a strong opening session on Thursday, when Anthropic shares surged 17% and closed at $97.17. The company's initial public offering became the largest on record, surpassing SpaceX's historic market debut in June. The Guardian reported that Anthropic reached a valuation of $1.7 trillion at the end of its first trading day.

However, the listing did little to ease concerns about the enormous capital expenditure required to build AI infrastructure. Investors have increasingly questioned whether companies investing billions of dollars in artificial intelligence can generate sufficient returns to justify their spending.

Across Asia, Taiwan's stock market suffered one of the sharpest declines. The benchmark fell 6.7%, reaching its lowest level since mid-April and extending its weekly losses beyond 16%. The decline put the market on course for its worst five-day performance since 1990.
According to The Guardian, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), the country's largest and most valuable listed company, lost approximately 6%.

South Korean equities also weakened, falling more than 5% to their lowest level in over nine months. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix each declined approximately 7%, adding to pressure on the region's technology sector.

sum: Chinese pharmaceutical stocks have been sluggish since November, even as policymakers have released a dense stream of positive news—a striking divergence. The A-share SW Pharmaceutical & Biotech Index and Hong Kong's Hang Seng Healthcare Index have pulled back in tandem, with declines concentrated in innovative drugs and the CXO complex, the most crowded trades of the year. Chen Chen, head of China healthcare research at UBS Securities, said at a recent media briefing that the sector has shown an earnings inflection point, and identified biotech, CRO and AI drug discovery as the three key areas to watch, arguing that China's pharmaceutical industry is shifting from reliance on the domestic market toward a new paradigm of "innovation plus globalization."

According to China Merchants Securities, the SW Pharmaceutical & Biotech Index fell 2.87% from November 9 to 13, underperforming the CSI 300 Index by 1.93 percentage points and ranking 26th among the 31 SW first-tier industry sectors. In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng Healthcare Index fell 1.61% over the same period but still outperformed the Hang Seng Index by 1.84 percentage points. The Hong Kong healthcare correction extended into this week; as of the November 17 close, the Hang Seng Healthcare Index stood at 3,470.87 points, down further from 3,559.03 on November 13.

Within the sector, the correction has been uneven. A-share pharmaceutical sub-sectors fell almost across the board, with vaccines, brick-and-mortar pharmacies and other biological products leading the declines. Chen Chen attributed the pullback to the large gains innovative drugs had accumulated earlier; with the interim earnings season over and catalysts from some overseas academic conferences having played out, the sector saw a period of profit-taking—a normal valuation digestion.

Notably, a flurry of recent policy moves failed to effectively support share prices. On November 14, China's National Healthcare Security Administration and the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security published the 2026 edition of the national medical insurance drug list and the commercial health insurance innovative drug list.

The company stressed in the announcement that its current order backlog is ample and that production and operations are proceeding normally as planned.

Enflame Technology said it is working with several Chinese semiconductor industry partners to build cloud AI chip products based on a Chinese-made supply chain, in order to establish a stable supply system and support business development.

On the day the announcement was released, Enflame Technology's shares closed at 364.33 yuan (approximately $54.72), down 20% for the session. The stock had fallen for four consecutive trading days: it hit a record high on Nov. 13, then declined steadily from Nov. 16 to Nov. 19.

items.t: Рекордные деньги вливаются в ETF, владеющие Anthropic, так кто же на самом деле покупает?
sum: The world’s biggest asset manager, BlackRock (NYSE:BLK | BLK Price Prediction), wants to put private companies inside a fund that trades like an ETF. The firm is seeking SEC approval for an exchange-traded interval fund, or ETIF. On Bloomberg’s ETF IQ, Dave Nadig, an ETF industry strategist, gave it a split decision: he likes the structure but is unsure of demand, as Eric Balchunas explained.

Meanwhile, the money already tracking private companies through ETFs comes mostly from professionals. Balchunas says ETFs holding private names like Anthropic and OpenAI account for just 0.2% of ETF assets but took in 30% of the flows last Thursday and Friday, and he says most of that buying came from hedge funds.

Balchunas wrote on Nov. 17 that the activity is “mostly hedge funds going long ETF and short the basket to isolate $ANT.” In this trade, a fund buys the ETF and sells short (sells borrowed shares of) the public stocks inside it. Those two positions cancel out, so the fund ends up holding only the piece it can’t buy directly, which is pre-IPO Anthropic.

Why go to the trouble? A post Balchunas shared said Anthropic’s planned IPO at a valuation of about $1.4 trillion points to higher marks for public funds whose reported valuations average about $1.07 trillion. That roughly 31% gap is what the hedge funds are trying to capture.

A day earlier, Balchunas called last Friday’s $23b in total ETF flows “absurd” compared with a $8b average. He described the buyers as a mix of Vanguard fans, dip buyers and “private co vultures” moving into ETFs that hold Anthropic ahead of its IPO.

Alger Concentrated Equity ETF (NYSEARCA:CNEQ) is the clearest case. Its June 30[1] holdings report lists Anthropic PBC at 5.28% of net assets, a position worth $38.65 million. The fund held $731.5 million in net assets at the time.

T. Rowe Price Capital Appreciation Equity ETF (NYSEARCA:TCAF) is harder to pin down. Balchunas named it alongside CNEQ, but its June 30[2] report, covering $7.4 billion in net assets, lists no position under Anthropic’s name.

items.t: Morgan Stanley оптимистичен в отношении акций A, медвежий в отношении акций Гонконга и расходится с Goldman Sachs
sum: Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs have issued opposing recommendations on China equity allocation for 2027. Morgan Stanley's November 15 China equity strategy outlook maintained an equal-weight rating on MSCI China and expressed a clear preference for A-shares over offshore markets such as Hong Kong stocks; Goldman Sachs, in its November 16 report, upgraded Hong Kong stocks to overweight and downgraded A-shares to neutral. The two institutions' views on relative A/H-share allocation are in direct opposition.

Morgan Stanley strategists including Laura Wang set base-case targets for end-2027: a Hang Seng Index of 26,000, implying 8% upside from the November 12 close; an HSCEI of 8,700, also implying 8% upside; MSCI China at 76, implying 11% upside; and the CSI 300 at 4,550, implying 13% upside. The bank believes modest earnings improvement, slight yuan appreciation and more reasonable valuations will provide structural support for Chinese equities, but weak domestic demand, cautious policy and intensifying US-China tech friction will cap index-level upside.

On earnings forecasts, Morgan Stanley is notably more conservative than the market. It expects MSCI China earnings per share to grow 8% in 2027, up from 6% in 2026 but far below the 14% consensus; it forecasts 10% earnings growth for the CSI 300, also well below the 19% consensus.
Note: Data from Morgan Stanley's 2027 China equity strategy outlook.

The analysts wrote in the report: "Our 2027 forecasts remain below bottom-up consensus, leaving room for further downward revisions, particularly concentrated in the remainder of 2026 and the first half of 2027." They expect analysts to reassess domestic demand, the distribution of AI capital spending and the impact of US-China tech restrictions after the US midterm elections, at which point consensus estimates will go through a front-loaded downgrade cycle.

Factors supporting earnings improvement include export resilience, continued AI and tech capital spending, the drag from price competition gradually fading from a low base, and translation gains from modest yuan appreciation.

sum: Chinese stocks closed lower on Monday (16 November), nearing their lowest level since July 2025. Concerns over whether the artificial intelligence (AI) rally can be sustained weighed on investor sentiment and sent hardware stocks lower, while renewed signs of weakness in China's economy deepened the market's pessimism.
Reuters reported that China's blue-chip CSI 300 Index and the Shanghai Composite Index both closed down 0.9% on Monday, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index rose 0.5%.

Asian technology stocks endured sharp swings the previous week, as the departure of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang following a series of scandals caught markets off guard. Nvidia is due to report earnings this week, while US AI company Anthropic is set to hold its initial public offering (IPO). Investors will look to both events for indications of whether the AI-driven bull market can broaden further.

Chinese AI hardware stocks fell sharply. The 5G communications index plunged 7.5% to its lowest level in a year, while the technology-heavy STAR 50 Index tumbled 5.2%. Shares in Zhongji Innolight, a major supplier of high-speed optical modules for AI data centres, slumped 12.3%.

Analysts said the upheaval at Nvidia could mark a turning point for Chinese chipmakers. If Washington tightens export controls in response to the turmoil, it could accelerate China's investment in domestically produced AI chips and computing infrastructure.

Meanwhile, China's economy showed renewed signs of weakness in October, with industrial output growth slowing and consumption remaining sluggish. The National Bureau of Statistics said on Monday that value-added industrial output at enterprises above a designated size rose 4.8% year on year in real terms in October, while total retail sales of consumer goods grew 0.4%. Both figures fell short of expectations, while investment continued to decline.
The CSI 300 Index has fallen 14% so far this year. However, amid broad declines in A-shares, the CSI 300 Financials Index rose 1.5%, while the consumer staples sector gained 1.2%.

items.t: Акции оборудования для искусственного интеллекта резко упали: акции Zhongji Innolight упали на 12,3% за один день, поскольку китайские акции достигли 16-месячного минимума
sum: Chinese stocks closed lower on Monday (the 16th), with AI hardware shares suffering the steepest declines and becoming the main drag on the broader market. The CSI 300 Index and the Shanghai Composite Index both fell 0.9% at the close, approaching their lowest levels since July 2025. Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index bucked the trend to close up 0.5%, diverging from the mainland market.

The rout was led by the AI supply chain, with the 5G communications index plunging 7.5% in a single day to a one-year low, while the STAR 50 Index sank 5.2%. Among individual names, Zhongji Innolight (300308-CN), a major maker of high-speed optical transceiver modules for AI data centers, saw heavy selling during the session and closed down 12.3%, a decline that stood out among large-cap stocks. Concerns over whether the AI investment boom can be sustained have risen markedly, and combined with the latest Chinese economic data showing weakening manufacturing production momentum and persistently sluggish domestic consumption, investor confidence has been visibly shaken.

The selling was not confined to China but extended the broad weakness in Asian AI hardware stocks. Last week, Nvidia (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang abruptly resigned, shocking the market and forcing investors to reassess the direction of U.S. AI chip export policy and the industry's outlook. Nvidia shares fell 13% for the week, wiping $573 billion off its market value in one stroke — the largest weekly decline since U.S. President Trump announced "reciprocal tariffs" in April last year.

Two more things are on the market's radar: Nvidia's upcoming earnings report and the initial public offering (IPO) that AI startup Anthropic is expected to launch this week. Both will serve as bellwethers for whether AI investment enthusiasm can be sustained.

Notably, a further tightening of U.S. chip export controls could paradoxically become a catalyst for China's semiconductor self-sufficiency. Jeff Ko, chief analyst at ViaBTC, noted that if Washington strengthens export restrictions in the wake of the Nvidia management upheaval, it could spur China to expand investment in domestic AI chips and computing infrastructure, creating new demand for China's semiconductor supply chain.

sum: Goldman Sachs adjusted its regional allocation in its newly published 2027 China market strategy outlook, upgrading Hong Kong stocks from neutral to "overweight" while cutting A-shares from overweight to neutral. The bank set an end-2027 target for the MSCI China Index implying roughly 23% upside, and a CSI 300 target of 4,500 points, implying gains of about 10%.

The analysis team led by Kinger Lau said plainly in the report that the MSCI China Index currently trades at just 9.8x 12-month forward earnings, about one standard deviation below its ten-year average, and that "a great deal of negative news is already in the price." The report's core judgment is that the main axis of trading in Chinese equities will undergo a structural shift in 2027: away from betting on AI beta and toward pursuing earnings growth, cash returns and diversified allocation.
AI Hard-Tech Profit Growth Decelerates; A-Share Estimates Face Downgrades

The key support for this allocation shift lies in the difference in earnings structure between the two markets. Goldman Sachs estimates that earnings growth for A-share AI hard-tech names will slow sharply from 85% in 2026 to 46% in 2027, and that this segment currently accounts for as much as 40% of CSI 300 Index earnings weight—so any deceleration in growth would have a very direct impact on the index.

At the same time, sell-side consensus estimates for A-shares are notably optimistic. Goldman Sachs forecasts 2027 earnings growth of 12% for the CSI 300 and 15% for the MSCI China Index, both below the 18% market consensus. The bank also noted that actual A-share earnings growth has fallen short of expectations for seven consecutive years, and that this "inertial characteristic" means consensus estimates carry downside revision risk.

The situation for Hong Kong stocks is the opposite. Goldman Sachs believes Hong Kong earnings will grow above trend, driven mainly by the internet sector and the broader soft-tech segment. Internet sector earnings growth is expected to accelerate from negative 3% in 2026 to 18% in 2027, while soft tech is seen speeding up from 14% to 22%.

sum: - Asian stocks tumbled on Tuesday led by chipmakers, with South Korea’s Kospi diving more than 6% below 6,000 to its lowest since July 31 and the Nikkei down 2.6%, as oil near two-week highs on Middle East conflict lifted the dollar and yields.

The Kospi’s heavy weighting toward chipmakers made it the region’s most exposed market, so the depth of the drop reflects both AI rally fatigue and concentrated positioning unwinding. A firm dollar adds pressure on Asian currencies and on foreign flows into regional equities. US bank earnings and this week’s CPI data (preview, another preview) are the next tests, and any sign that energy costs are feeding into broader inflation would reinforce the hawkish rate outlook weighing on growth stocks.
Asia’s AI darlings took the brunt of a nervous day, as oil reminded markets that geopolitics bites hardest when it feeds into inflation and higher rates.

sum: Mainland Chinese stocks opened higher but slid in the afternoon as optical-module and circuit-board makers sold off on Nvidia’s leadership turmoil, while banks hit record highs and kept the Shanghai benchmark well ahead of Shenzhen.

The Shanghai Composite Index closed at 3,634.35 points on Friday 13 November 2026, down 21.48 points or 0.59%. It was the index’s second straight decline after a 0.67% fall to 3,655.83 on Thursday, and it left the benchmark back below its five-day and ten-day moving averages. The session range ran from 3,623.84 to 3,669.44.

The headline loss understates the damage across the wider market. The Shenzhen Component Index fell 2.05% to 10,968.79, the growth-focused ChiNext Index slid 3.32% to 2,426.08, the STAR 50 lost 2.30% to 1,279.66 and the blue-chip CSI 300 eased 0.68% to 4,016.29. More than 4,700 stocks declined against roughly 750 that rose, and combined Shanghai and Shenzhen turnover shrank to about 1.66 trillion yuan, around 276 billion yuan less than on Thursday.

A-shares opened higher and the Shanghai Composite traded in positive territory through the morning, briefly rising about 0.2% towards 3,663. The tone changed sharply after the lunch break, when selling hit the computing-hardware complex and the index fell almost 1% at its worst before trimming losses into the close.

The dominant story of the session was the abrupt exit of Jensen Huang, the co-founder who had led Nvidia since 1993. The company said on Thursday that he had stepped down as president, chief executive and board member with immediate effect, following reports of multiple affairs, including one with a woman US intelligence suspects of spying for China. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO, Harvey C. Jones becomes the company’s first independent chairman, and Nvidia is due to report quarterly results next week. Nvidia shares opened as much as 14% lower on Thursday before closing down 4.34%, and extended losses on Friday after HSBC downgraded the stock.

Chinese suppliers of optical modules, printed circuit boards and electronic components have been among the biggest beneficiaries of US AI data-centre spending, so the uncertainty around Nvidia’s strategy hit them hardest.

sum: China is scrambling to contain a stock-market rout only two years after the previous rescue.

Beijing is dusting off the market-support playbook it deployed in 2024. The People’s Bank of China is providing low-cost funding for corporate share buybacks and liquidity for institutional investors. The shadowy “national team” appears to have stepped up its operations, while regulators are again resorting to window guidance — informally instructing institutional investors and brokerages not to sell.

In October, China’s stock market suffered its worst monthly decline in more than a decade. The blue-chip CSI 300 Index has fallen into a bear market from its late-June peak, while Shanghai’s semiconductor-heavy SSE Science and Technology Innovation Board 50 Index, or Star 50, has plunged as much as 48%.

Liang certainly has reason to deflect blame. China has a long history of faulting private-sector investors, from quant funds to foreign asset managers, for igniting selloffs. But he might just have a point this time.

China had already endured a bear market in July, when momentum-driven trades suffered their worst loss in history. The pattern mirrored markets in South Korea and the US, where the red-hot semiconductor trade was hastily unwound. Three months later, however, the usual suspects are harder to blame. Margin financing has already fallen, as has northbound turnover through the Stock Connect with Hong Kong, suggesting neither leveraged traders nor foreign hot money is behind the latest weakness. That leaves a different potential offender: long-only institutional investors.

State-owned insurers have been steadily increasing their stock holdings in recent years. China Life Insurance Co., for instance, has scaled up artificial-intelligence-related bets and raised its equity allocation to 19.2% of its portfolio by the end of June, from 16.9% in 2025. Beyond the hunt for higher returns, insurers have been responding to policymakers, who want them to provide more long-term capital to the stock market — a priority that the head of China’s securities regulator reiterated in a high-profile speech in mid-June. Talk about bad timing.

sum: Following a broad sell-off in AI stocks, investors began reallocating capital to previously out-of-favor markets in China and India. Fund managers are looking for opportunities in sectors less dependent on AI infrastructure, Bloomberg reported.

The shift in strategy followed the U.S. midterm elections, in which Democrats gained control of both chambers of Congress. Bloomberg said market participants feared tighter AI regulation and reassessed the payback of multibillion-dollar investments in data centers. Against this backdrop, on November 5 the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.52%.

The next day, following U.S. indexes, Japan’s Nikkei 225 and South Korea’s KOSPI fell by about 6%. Asian technology shares came under the most pressure. Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing supply equipment for AI infrastructure, so their business largely depends on spending by U.S. corporations.

For the week, India’s Nifty 50 gained 8.6%, its best performance since February 2021. The Sensex rose 8.8%. Reuters noted that on November 6 both indexes closed at their highest levels in more than eight months.

The rally was fueled by foreign inflows. According to Bloomberg, over the four days through November 4, foreign investors put about $1.9 billion into Indian equities. During the next trading session, funds’ net purchases reached $1.6 billion — the highest one-day total in nearly six years.

Bloomberg also cited the structure of India’s stock market: AI hardware makers have a relatively small weight in local indexes. Charlie Hong, investment director at LOGOS Asset Management, told Bloomberg that in October he sold SK Hynix, Samsung Electronics, Intel and Lumentum. He increased allocations to Indian technology companies, financials and drug manufacturers.
Banks led gains. According to Reuters, India’s financial sector added 10.4% for the week, HDFC Bank rose 13.8%, and ICICI Bank gained 12.4%.

The South Korean stock market has come under massive pressure amid a global sell-off of tech stocks. As a result, the benchmark KOSPI index plummeted by more than 8 percent in early trading.

Shares of memory chip manufacturers SK Hynix (-11 percent) and Samsung Electronics (-8 percent) also fell sharply. Investors appeared to be reacting to the losses on Wall Street, where concerns about the future of investment in artificial intelligence weighed on stock prices. This comes against the backdrop of the Democrats’ victory in the U.S. midterm elections, which heightened fears of a possible slowdown in the expansion of data centers. Due to their high financing requirements and potential environmental damage, the expansion of new data centers in the United States is facing increasing resistance.

In addition, the South Korean news agency Yonhap cited the risk of rising oil prices as another reason for the market declines, following reports from Iran that several tankers had once again been damaged in the Strait of Hormuz. As an energy-poor industrialized nation, South Korea is heavily reliant on oil imports from the Middle East. At the same time, its stock market is particularly vulnerable to fluctuations in the AI sector due to the semiconductor industry’s significant weight in the market.

Japan's leading index, the Nikkei 225, fell by about 6.5 percent in early trading. sum: Efforts stepped up to bolster capital market liquidity and stability

China's financial regulators are stepping up efforts to bolster capital market liquidity and stability, with the central bank preparing a fresh round of funding support for institutional investors and the securities regulator moving to encourage more share buybacks and attract additional long-term capital.

The People's Bank of China announced on Monday that it would conduct a new round of operations under its securities, funds and insurance companies swap facility (SFISF) on Tuesday to support the sound and stable development of the capital market.

The move will have a one-year tenor, with possible extensions, the PBOC said in a statement. So far, 31 securities and fund management firms have applied for more than 100 billion yuan ($15 billion) under the operation.

Introduced in 2024, the facility allows eligible securities firms, fund managers and insurers to swap assets including bonds, stock exchange-traded funds and CSI 300 Index constituent shares for highly liquid assets such as government bonds and central bank bills.
The funds obtained should be used exclusively for capital market investments, including stock and stock ETF investments and market-making.

Lou Feipeng, a researcher at Postal Savings Bank of China, said the new SFISF operation will provide nonbanking financial institutions with liquidity support that can help break the vicious cycle of redemptions and forced sell-offs, facilitating countercyclical share purchases during market downturns without expanding the monetary base.

sum: Mainland Chinese stocks extended a technology-led slide on Friday 30 October 2026, with the Shanghai benchmark posting its lowest close since August 2025 and the CSI 300 recording a record 12th straight weekly decline.

The Shanghai Stock Exchange Composite Index closed at 3,599.02 on Friday 30 October 2026, down 52.42 points or 1.44% from Thursday's close of 3,651.43, according to figures reported by Xinhua and confirmed by Morningstar's Dow Jones Market Data. The index opened roughly 1.3% lower near 3,605 and spent the session under pressure, closing just below the psychologically important 3,600 level.

The close marks a new 52-week closing low for the benchmark and its lowest finish since 4 August 2025. Friday's loss came on top of a 0.82% decline on Thursday, meaning the index has dropped more than 2.2% across the final two sessions of the month.

The immediate catalyst was a global retreat from artificial intelligence and semiconductor shares after Amazon and Intel released disappointing quarterly updates in the United States. Intel warned of a weak fourth quarter on the back of a slump in personal computer demand, while Amazon's results and holiday-quarter guidance missed expectations. These reports followed Alphabet's steep fall on Thursday and deepened doubts about how quickly heavy AI spending will translate into profits.

Mainland China's growth boards are particularly sensitive to that narrative. Computing-power hardware and memory-chip companies, which had attracted heavy domestic retail and institutional buying earlier in the year, were sold aggressively for a second straight day. The pain was far worse outside the main Shanghai board: the ChiNext growth index in Shenzhen plunged about 4.1% on Friday after sinking 4.45% on Thursday.

The SSE Composite, which covers all A and B shares listed in Shanghai and includes a large weighting in banks, energy and state-owned industrials, therefore fell less than the technology-heavy gauges. Even so, losses of this size on a broad, value-tilted index reflect how widely the risk-off mood spread through mainland portfolios.
October was the SSE Composite's weakest month in a considerable time. The index lost 243.18 points, or 6.33%, during the month, according to Dow Jones Market Data.
